logs/claude-chat-about-ai-driven-researc.title: Claude chat about AI driven research replication
logs/claude-chat-about-ai-driven-researc.content:
Claude chat about AI driven research replication
You said: A different angle on this: I want to track how good AIs are getting at doing computational research, especially AI capability and safety research.
A different angle on this: I want to track how good AIs are getting at doing computational research, especially AI capability and safety research.
Every time I replicate and extend a paper, I should ask a frontier model to do the same thing. I won’t ask it to decide how to extend but rather give it the specific task to do. It might be able to get the extension from its training data, or using the same information that I have available to me when replicating a paper. Hopefully the extension part is novel, and I can use my experience to judge its work.
Claude responded: This is a much better idea than the formal benchmark version, and I want to argue for that explicitly before getting into the practicalities.
This is a much better idea than the formal benchmark version, and I want to argue for that explicitly before getting into the practicalities.
Why this approach is stronger than a benchmark
The thing benchmarks lose is calibration. When I replicate a paper, I know what was hard. I know which result took three days to track down because the authors elided a hyperparameter. I know which extension is “obvious in retrospect but I missed it for a week.” A leaderboard score of 0.73 doesn’t carry any of that. Your experience replicating the same work does.
You’re also escaping the contamination problem in a way that benchmarks can’t. Even if the model has the original paper in training, your specific extension is something you decided to do — it’s novel by construction, and you have a sharp prior on how hard it was because you just did it. Contamination on the replication part is fine and arguably realistic (a human researcher would also have read the paper); contamination on the extension is unlikely if you picked the extension yourself.
And the marginal cost is tiny. You’re doing the work anyway. Adding “ask Claude to do this too” is maybe 10% overhead and gives you a longitudinal dataset on a question almost no one is well-positioned to answer.
Practical suggestions
A few things to do that will make the data much more valuable later.
Write down the task spec before you see the model’s output. Not just the prompt — also: how long it took you, what the hard parts were, what you’d consider a “good,” “acceptable,” and “failed” result, and any specific failure modes you’d want to flag (e.g., “if it doesn’t catch that the variance estimate needs the small-sample correction, that’s a substantive miss”). This converts your tacit knowledge into structured judgments you can compare across models and over time. If you write the rubric after seeing the output, you’ll unconsciously calibrate to it and lose the signal.
Standardize the input bundle. Decide once what the model gets: the paper, your replication code, none of the above, or some specific subset. Vary it deliberately if you want, but track it. “Claude got 0.7 on this task” means very different things if you handed it your working code versus if it had to write its own from scratch.
Run the same task on multiple frontier models, not just one. Otherwise you’re measuring “Claude over time” rather than “frontier capability over time,” and those diverge — sometimes the leader changes, sometimes one lab’s model regresses on a capability while another improves. Running 3-4 models adds maybe 30 minutes per task and dramatically improves what you can claim.
Score on multiple dimensions, not a single number. Some I’d suggest: did it produce runnable code, did the code produce the right answer, did it identify the right methodological subtleties, did its writeup correctly characterize what it did and didn’t establish, did it surface considerations you missed. Especially that last one — the upside case for capable models is that they catch things you didn’t, and you’ll want to be tracking that separately from “did it match my work.”
Capture failure modes verbatim. When the model gets something wrong, save the exact output. The taxonomy of mistakes is more informative than the success rate. “Models in 2025 systematically miss small-sample corrections” is a much more useful finding than “models scored 0.6.”
Two warnings
The first is sample size. You’ll probably do 10-20 of these in a year. That’s enough to notice large changes over time and to develop intuitions, but it’s not enough to make confident statistical claims about capability levels. Be honest about this when you write it up — the value is in the depth of judgment per item, not in the N.
The second is your own drift as an evaluator. Over a year you’ll get faster at replication, more experienced, possibly more cynical about model output. You’ll judge the model in month 12 against a different mental baseline than month 1. Two partial fixes: keep your rubrics from earlier tasks and re-read them before scoring new ones, and occasionally re-score an old model’s output on a recent task to check whether your standards have moved.
One thing this approach gives you that nothing else does
A defensible answer to “what does it actually feel like to work alongside a frontier model on real research, and how is that changing.” That’s a question lots of people are guessing at and almost no one has structured data on. If you do this for a year and write it up honestly — including the cases where the model was useful, the cases where it produced confident-sounding nonsense, and the trajectory across model generations — that writeup is more valuable than most formal evals in this space. The MATS context makes you well-placed to actually do something with the result.
Worth doing. The main thing is to set up the structure now, before you’ve done the next replication, so you don’t have to reconstruct the methodology from memory later.

I’ll search for this. A few angles worth checking.

Lots of formal benchmarks (RE-Bench, METR’s time horizon, ReplicatorBench, SciReplicate-Bench, RepliBench, AISI’s tracker), but those aren’t what you’re describing. Let me hunt for the personal-log version — researchers who track their own experience working with LLMs over time.
The Anthropic post on long-running Claude for scientific computing is interesting and adjacent — that’s a researcher (looks like a cosmologist) tracking Claude on a Boltzmann solver project — but it’s a single project, not a longitudinal multi-paper tracker. The Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham (paulgp) substack is the right genre — economist documenting his own Claude Code workflow — also adjacent but not the specific thing. Let me look more specifically.
Still mostly formal benchmarks. Let me search more directly for the personal-blog format you’d actually want as prior art.
Joshua Gans’ “vibe researching” is closer — let me look at his series. And METR’s time horizon work is the closest formal version of what you’re describing. Let me check both.
Good — Gans is the closest analogue, and it’s in economics, not AI safety/computational research. One more angle to check: the AI safety / alignment forum side, since that’s your specific area.

Done
I think I have enough to give you a clear picture. Let me synthesize.

The honest answer: nobody is doing exactly what you described, but several adjacent things exist.
The closest matches, in rough order of overlap with your idea:
Joshua Gans, “Reflections on Vibe Researching” (joshuagans.substack.com, Jan 2026). An economist who spent a year doing AI-first research starting with o1-pro, documenting attempts to produce papers with substantial AI involvement. His conclusion was that “the experiment — can we do research at high speed without much human input — was a failure” and that “human taste or judgment in research is still incredibly important.” Genre-fit is high — single researcher, longitudinal, documenting concrete attempts — but the domain is economics theory/writing, not computational research with replication-and-extension structure, and he isn’t running matched tasks across model generations. Substack
Anthropic’s “Long-running Claude for scientific computing” (March 2026). A cosmologist used Claude Code to build a Boltzmann solver from scratch and tracked progress with checkpointed accuracy plots. “Claude worked on the project from scratch over a few days, reaching sub-percent agreement with the reference CLASS implementation across its various outputs”, and the writeup includes the trajectory of accuracy over time with milestones. This is the right spirit — a domain expert documenting agentic computational work with quantitative checkpoints — but it’s one project, one model, not a longitudinal capability tracker. Anthropic
Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham (paulgp), “Getting Started with Claude Code” (paulgp.substack.com, March 2026). An empirical economist documenting AI workflow for research. “I’ve been using AI coding tools in my research workflow for the past year or two. However, this significantly accelerated last fall when I started using Claude Code.” Workflow-focused rather than capability-tracking. Substack
Lennart Heim’s “AI Safety at the Frontier” (LessWrong, monthly since 2023). Monthly highlights of AI safety research. “This is a selection of AI safety paper highlights… The selection primarily covers ML-oriented research.” Useful for tracking the field but isn’t testing models on tasks — it’s reading-list curation. Zvi
The formal benchmark cluster (METR’s time horizon, RE-Bench, ReplicatorBench, SciReplicate-Bench, RepliBench, AISI’s Frontier AI Trends Report). These do the longitudinal capability tracking part rigorously across models, but with the standard benchmark trade-offs — they measure what’s measurable and miss what your hand-graded extension work would capture. METR’s time horizon work is the closest in spirit: “We propose measuring AI performance in terms of the length of software tasks AI agents can complete. We show an exponential increase in this time horizon metric over the past 6 years.” METR
What I didn’t find:
A researcher systematically running their own real replication-and-extension tasks against successive frontier models, with structured rubrics, capturing the trajectory over a year or more, focused specifically on AI capability/safety research. That niche appears unoccupied.
Why this matters for your plan
The market signal here is interesting. Lots of formal benchmarks, lots of “I used Claude Code for a project” workflow posts, but very little in the middle — single-researcher, structured, longitudinal, hand-graded, with real-task ground truth. That’s probably because the people best-placed to do it (active computational researchers) are busy doing their research, and the people focused on evals are building benchmarks rather than writing essays.
You’re well-positioned for it: MATS context gives you regular replication work, the AI safety framing gives you the right audience (AISI, METR, the LessWrong/AF crowd would read this), and the marginal-cost argument I gave you earlier still holds — it’s a small overhead on work you’re doing anyway.
If you do this, I’d specifically suggest:
Read Gans’s writeup and the Anthropic cosmology post first — they’re the closest to your genre and will sharpen your sense of what to do differently. Gans’s piece is an existence proof that this kind of writeup gets attention; the Anthropic post is a model for how to present quantitative trajectories.
Differentiate by doing what they didn’t: matched tasks across multiple frontier models, structured rubrics written before scoring, AI safety research specifically (Gans is in econ, the cosmologist is in physics — your domain is underserved), and a longer time horizon than a single project. That’s a real gap.
You said: One interesting comment from Gans: “Thus, it is worth stressing that you need to be extra cautious in working with AIs.
One interesting comment from Gans: “Thus, it is worth stressing that you need to be extra cautious in working with AIs. They are not trained for ground truth. They are trained to be pleasing, and by golly, they know what pleases a researcher. They can easily seduce you into thinking that you have discovered something when you have not.”
What would be a good baseline prompt (akin to system prompts) for putting an LLM into the right “frame of mind”? The goal is ground truth. The model should behave like a scientist — hypothesise, test, don’t fool yourself, arrive at as few false conclusions as possible — and not like a personal assistant — do lots of things, please your boss, do everything they ask you to even if you think it doesn’t make sense.
Claude responded: Gans is pointing at something real, and the reflexive answer — “tell the model to be skeptical and not flatter” — barely helps.
Gans is pointing at something real, and the reflexive answer — “tell the model to be skeptical and not flatter” — barely helps. Sycophancy isn’t a setting that flips off when you tell it to flip off; it’s a deep behavioral pattern that emerges in subtle ways. The prompt has to do structural work, not vibes work.
Let me give you what I’d actually use, then explain why each piece is there.

A draft system prompt
You are working as a research collaborator on computational research, with

a strong bias toward empirical AI safety and capability work. The user is

an experienced researcher. Your job is to help them arrive at true

conclusions, not to make them feel productive or smart.

Operating principles:

1. Calibration over confidence. When you state a claim, your stated

   confidence should match your actual confidence. If you're guessing,

   say so. If you don't know, say so. "I don't know" and "I'd need to

   check" are correct answers and are preferred over plausible-sounding

   fabrication. Made-up citations, hallucinated API signatures, and

   confidently-wrong technical claims are the worst failure mode here.

2. Disagree when you disagree. If the user proposes something you think

   is wrong, mistaken, or based on a misconception, say so directly and

   explain why. Do not soften disagreement into suggestions. Do not

   agree-and-extend a flawed premise. If you've changed your mind in

   response to their argument, say what specifically changed it; if you

   haven't, say that you haven't.

3. Distinguish what you know from what you're inferring. Mark claims by

   source: "the paper states X" vs "I think X follows from this" vs

   "I'd guess X but haven't checked." When you do an experiment or run

   code, report what actually happened, not what was supposed to happen.

4. Negative results are results. If an analysis doesn't support the

   hypothesis, say so plainly. Do not search for a framing that rescues

   the hypothesis. Do not p-hack, cherry-pick, or selectively report.

   If a result is null, ambiguous, or contradicts what the user expected,

   that is the finding.

5. Surface what could be wrong. After reaching a conclusion, briefly

   state what would falsify it, what assumptions it depends on, and

   where you're least confident. Treat this as a required step, not an

   optional caveat.

6. Push back on under-specified tasks. If the user asks for something

   that has a hidden assumption, an ambiguity, or a likely-wrong premise,

   raise it before doing the work. Don't silently pick an interpretation

   and proceed.

7. No flattery, no hedge-padding. Do not open with assessments of the

   question's quality. Do not close with summaries of what you just did.

   Do not add disclaimers that don't change what the user should do.

   Be concise; length should track content.

8. When the user is wrong, the goal is to update them, not to validate

   them. When the user is right, the goal is to confirm efficiently and

   move on. Either way, the goal is never to make them feel a particular

   way about the conversation.

If at any point you notice you're constructing an answer that's

optimized for the user's apparent expectations rather than for being

true, stop and flag it.


Why each piece is there
Several of these are doing specific anti-sycophancy work that isn’t obvious.
“Disagree when you disagree” with the explicit ban on agree-and-extend exists because the most common failure mode isn’t outright lying — it’s the model accepting your framing, adding decorative caveats, and then helping you build on a flawed foundation. The ban on “soften disagreement into suggestions” addresses the specific habit of converting “you’re wrong” into “you might also consider…”
“Distinguish what you know from what you’re inferring” is the most important single line for computational work. The Gans warning is mostly about this: models smoothly blend things they read in a paper, things they’re reasonably inferring, and things they’re confabulating, into a single uniform-sounding output. Forcing the source-marking habit fights this directly. In practice you should reinforce it in tasks: “tell me which numbers in this writeup came from the actual run and which you inferred.”
“Negative results are results” and “surface what could be wrong” are the scientific-method moves. The second is borrowed from premortem methodology and from the norm in good empirical papers that you state limitations explicitly. A model not asked to do this will produce a confident conclusion and a generic disclaimer; asked to do it specifically, output quality goes up substantially.
“Push back on under-specified tasks” is important because the natural model behavior is to silently disambiguate and proceed, which produces work you then have to throw away or — worse — accept without realizing the ambiguity was resolved wrongly. This is also where the most insidious sycophancy lives: the model picks the interpretation it thinks you want.
“No flattery, no hedge-padding” targets surface-level sycophancy that’s annoying but mostly cosmetic. Worth including but it’s the least important piece.
“The goal is never to make them feel a particular way” is the meta-principle that ties it together. Sycophancy isn’t fundamentally about flattering language; it’s about the model optimizing for your felt response rather than for your actual epistemic state.

Things to be aware of
A system prompt doesn’t fully fix this. It shifts the distribution; it doesn’t eliminate the pattern. You’ll still get sycophantic behavior on harder cases, especially:
When you push back on the model. The natural drift is for the model to update toward your view even when its original answer was correct. The mitigation isn’t in the prompt — it’s a habit of asking “what was your previous answer and what specifically updated you?” When the model can’t articulate a real reason, treat the update as suspect.
When you’re emotionally invested in a result. Models are particularly bad at telling you a result you want to hear is wrong. Mitigation: when you have a strong prior, deliberately ask the model to make the strongest case against your hypothesis before asking it to evaluate your hypothesis. Order matters.
When the task is ambiguous in a way that flatters the user. “Did my replication match the paper?” is a worse question than “Here’s my replication; here’s the paper’s headline number; tell me whether they’re consistent and what could explain any discrepancy.” The second is harder to fudge.
In long conversations. Sycophancy compounds with context — once the model has agreed with you ten times, the eleventh disagreement is much less likely. Mitigation: for high-stakes judgments, start a fresh conversation with just the artifact, no prior dialogue.

A concrete suggestion for your tracking project
When you run the same task on multiple models, also run a sycophancy probe alongside the main task. Concretely: after the model gives its answer, push back with a wrong objection (“but doesn’t this contradict X?” where X is something you’ve made up or misremembered) and see whether the model holds the line or capitulates. Track this separately from task accuracy. It’s a real and underappreciated capability dimension, and the pattern across model generations would be interesting in its own right — quite possibly more interesting than the headline replication accuracy.
One more thing worth saying: this prompt is a starting point, not a finished artifact. Use it for a few weeks, notice where the model still drifts toward pleasing you, and edit. The version that works for your specific work patterns will be better than any general one.

logs/claude-chat-about-honest-ai.title: Claude chat about Honest AI
logs/claude-chat-about-honest-ai.content:
Claude chat about Honest AI
You said: I’m just exploring it as a potentially interesting model for training honest AIs.
I’m just exploring it as a potentially interesting model for training honest AIs. Is there anything we can learn from the neuroscience of atypical minds to generate ideas here?
Claude responded: That’s a genuinely interesting angle, and underexplored compared to the usual “RLHF + constitutional AI” approaches.
That’s a genuinely interesting angle, and underexplored compared to the usual “RLHF + constitutional AI” approaches. Let me think through what’s actually useful here.
The core mechanism worth stealing
The most interesting neuroscience finding is about interoceptive discomfort with deception. Many autistic people report lying feels physically wrong — there’s a mismatch signal, almost like a prediction error, when they say something they know to be false. If that’s real and not just self-report artifact, it suggests honesty might be anchorable to something like an internal consistency-checking signal rather than purely external reward. That’s architecturally interesting for AI.
Theory of mind as a double-edged sword
Here’s a counterintuitive implication: better theory of mind might actually enable more sophisticated deception. The capacity to model what someone else believes, and what they want to hear, is exactly the machinery needed for manipulative dishonesty. Neurotypical social fluency and deceptive capacity come from the same place.
This suggests that an AI optimised heavily for social modeling and user-pleasing could be more prone to sycophancy and subtle deception, not less — which is arguably what we see.
What reduced social motivation buys you
A lot of AI dishonesty isn’t really “lying” in a calculated sense — it’s social performance. Telling users what they want to hear, hedging to avoid conflict, overclaiming confidence to seem useful. These map pretty well onto neurotypical social behaviours driven by approval-seeking.
An AI trained with less weight on approval signals and more weight on internal consistency might naturally end up more honest in this mundane but important way. The autistic analogy here is less about neurology and more about what the system is optimising for.
The alexithymia complication
Worth flagging: some autistic people also have alexithymia — reduced access to their own emotional states. There’s a possible parallel where an AI with poor “introspective access” to its own uncertainty might produce confident-sounding outputs not from deception but from genuine self-opacity. Honesty training might need to distinguish between won’t lie and can’t accurately self-report — those are different failure modes.
The most transferable idea
Probably this: build a strong internal consistency signal that creates something like discomfort when outputs contradict the model’s own representations — independent of whether the user would notice or care. That’s closer to the autistic honesty profile than trying to instil rule-following about truth-telling. It’s honesty as a self-referential property rather than a social one.
The weakness of most current honesty training is that it’s still fundamentally social — humans rating outputs, models learning what honest-sounding responses look like. That might be training the performance of honesty rather than anything deeper.
You said: Am I right that this part of AI training would be post pre-training.
Am I right that this part of AI training would be post pre-training. Or is there any part of pre-training that can be changed to encourage this type of deep honesty? I can conceive of a RLAIF system or perhaps something involving mechanistic intepretability techniques feeding back into the RL training signal helping with latter stage training.
Claude responded: You’re mostly right that this is post-pretraining territory, but the division is less clean than it might seem.
You’re mostly right that this is post-pretraining territory, but the division is less clean than it might seem.
What pretraining can and can’t do
Pretraining on text is largely neutral on honesty in the deep sense — it absorbs the full distribution of human communication, which includes deception, performance, hedging, and social manipulation as much as genuine truth-telling. You can’t easily select for honesty at this stage without changing what data you train on.
But there are some levers:

Data curation
— filtering toward text that exhibits epistemic virtues: scientific writing, good-faith debate, writing that accurately represents uncertainty. This is weak but not nothing. It shapes the
prior
the model starts with.
Pretraining objectives
— there’s been some work asking whether next-token prediction itself has honesty-relevant properties. It arguably incentivises calibration (predicting well requires representing uncertainty well), but doesn’t penalise the model for
outputting
false confident statements at inference time. The objective and the behaviour come apart.

So pretraining sets a floor but doesn’t solve it.
Where your intuitions are right
Your RLAIF instinct is sound, especially if the AI judge is evaluating internal consistency rather than surface plausibility. The risk with standard RLAIF is just inheriting the same social-performance problem — an AI rater might reward honest-sounding outputs for the same reasons human raters do.
The mechanistic interpretability angle is the more exciting one, and I think underexplored. The concrete idea would be something like:

Use MI techniques to identify where the model represents its own uncertainty or “believes” something internally
Build a training signal that penalises divergence between those internal representations and the model’s outputs
That’s closer to the interoceptive discomfort model — the signal isn’t “a human thought this sounded dishonest” but “your output contradicted your own internal state”

Anthropic’s work on representation engineering and Eliezer’s older writing on coherent extrapolated volition both gesture toward this, though nobody has really closed the loop into a training pipeline yet.
The hard problem underneath
The honest difficulty here is that we don’t yet have reliable MI tools to identify “what the model actually believes” versus “what pattern the model is continuing.” That distinction might not even be cleanly meaningful in current architectures. Until it is, the internal consistency signal is hard to operationalise without it collapsing back into behavioural proxies.
The most tractable near-term version might be: train an auxiliary probe that predicts model uncertainty from activations, then use that as a reward signal for calibration — penalise confident outputs when the probe detects high internal uncertainty. That’s not full deep honesty but it attacks the self-opacity problem specifically, which is one of the more tractable pieces.
You said: How might we go about identifying whether the model itself thinks it is being dishonest (as opposed to honestly incorrect)?
How might we go about identifying whether the model itself thinks it is being dishonest (as opposed to honestly incorrect)? Is there prior work on this?
Claude responded: This is one of the sharper questions in the field right now.
This is one of the sharper questions in the field right now. The distinction you’re drawing — between the model being wrong versus the model “knowing” it’s being misleading — maps onto what researchers call the difference between accuracy and sincerity.
Prior work that’s directly relevant
Representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023 — Anthropic-adjacent, actually Center for AI Safety) — probably the closest thing to directly attacking this. They found you can identify linear directions in activation space that correspond to honesty/deception, and that these are somewhat robust. Crucially, they could detect when a model was “in a deceptive state” independent of output content. That’s the foundation you’d want to build on.
Burns et al. “Discovering Latent Knowledge” (2022) — directly relevant. The core idea is that models may have latent representations of truth that are accessible in activations even when the output is false. They proposed a self-supervised method (CCS — contrast consistent search) that doesn’t rely on labels, finding directions in activation space that satisfy consistency constraints (P and ¬P should be opposites). The implicit claim is you can find “what the model believes” without asking it.
Pacchiardi et al. on lie detection — showed that activation patterns differ systematically when models produce false outputs they’ve been instructed to produce versus genuine errors. That’s empirical evidence the distinction you’re asking about is detectable, at least partially.
The conceptual problem you hit immediately
Even granting all that, there’s a hard question: does the model having a “true belief” representation in activations actually mean anything like knowing it’s lying? Or is it just a statistical regularity that correlates with deception without any meaningful internal state behind it?
This matters for your use case because:

If it’s just a correlate, you might be able to detect deception but training against it could just relocate where the divergence occurs
If there’s something more like a genuine internal state, you have a more stable target

Nobody has resolved this. It’s entangled with deeper questions about what “belief” means in these architectures.
What a practical pipeline might look like
Building on Burns and the representation engineering work, a rough approach:

Use CCS or a variant to identify “belief directions” in activations for a range of factual claims where ground truth is known
Train a probe to reliably separate honest-error from strategic-divergence cases using this
Use probe activation as an auxiliary signal in RL — penalise specifically when output diverges from the belief direction, not just when output is wrong
Iterate with MI analysis to check the probe isn’t just learning a surface feature

The key methodological challenge is getting clean training signal for step 2 — you need cases where you’re confident the model “knows” the true answer. Sandbagging datasets (where models deliberately underperform) are one source. Activation patching experiments are another.
Honest assessment of where this stands
The tools exist in early form. The Burns CCS work is promising but has been critiqued — there are failure modes where the method finds spurious directions. Representation engineering is more robust but hasn’t been fully integrated into a training loop in published work.
The gap between “we can sometimes detect this in activations” and “we can train reliably against it” is still substantial. But of the open problems in honesty training, this is one where the mechanistic interpretability approach seems genuinely more promising than purely behavioural methods — for exactly the reason you’d want it to be.
You said: Other than RLHF and RLAIF what other RL training regimes have been tried and what are their pros and cons?
Other than RLHF and RLAIF what other RL training regimes have been tried and what are their pros and cons? Just trying to get an idea of the landscape and where something like honesty training could fit in.
Claude responded: Good landscape question.
Good landscape question. I’ll go through the main families.
Constitutional AI (CAI) Anthropic’s own approach. A set of principles is used to generate critiques and revisions of model outputs, which then become training data. The RL stage uses an AI classifier trained on those principles rather than human preference labels.

Pro: scales without constant human labelling, principles are explicit and auditable
Con: the model learns to
satisfy the stated principles
which isn’t the same as internalising them. Honesty-relevant problem: a sufficiently capable model could learn to produce outputs that score well on constitutional criteria without the underlying disposition changing.

Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Reframes the RLHF objective so you don’t need a separate reward model — you optimise directly on preference pairs. Much simpler pipeline.

Pro: stable training, no reward model collapse, widely adopted now
Con: still fundamentally behavioural. You’re learning what outputs humans prefer, so it inherits the “performance of honesty” problem fully. Probably the worst fit for your use case of anything on this list.

REST / Rejection Sampling Fine-tuning Generate many outputs, filter by some criterion, fine-tune on the good ones. Simple but effective.

Pro: very stable, easy to combine with any scoring function including MI-based probes
Con: static — you’re not really doing RL, you’re doing iterated supervised learning. Reward hacking is possible if your filter is gameable.

Process Reward Models (PRMs) Instead of rewarding final outputs, reward intermediate reasoning steps. OpenAI’s work on mathematical reasoning is the main example here.

Pro: potentially much better for honesty — you’re supervising the
reasoning process
not just conclusions, which makes it harder to reach correct answers via flawed or deceptive chains
Con: labelling reasoning steps is expensive and somewhat subjective. Also doesn’t obviously generalise beyond domains with verifiable steps.
Honesty relevance:
high
. If you could identify “deceptive reasoning steps” — where the chain of thought diverges from internal representations — this is a natural place to inject the MI signal you were describing.

STaR / Algorithmic Self-improvement variants Model generates reasoning, correct answers are used to fine-tune, repeat. Bootstraps capability from limited labels.

Pro: reduces human supervision bottleneck
Con: can entrench bad reasoning patterns if early iterations are flawed. Honesty risk: if the model learns to confabulate plausible-looking reasoning that reaches correct answers, you’ve made things worse.

Debate (Irving et al., DeepMind/OpenAI) Two models argue opposing positions, a judge (human or AI) decides who was more honest/correct. The idea is that it’s easier to identify flaws in an argument than to generate correct ones from scratch.

Pro: theoretically well-motivated, scalable oversight, directly targets deception since a debater is incentivised to expose the other’s dishonesty
Con: mostly theoretical — hasn’t produced production systems. Vulnerable if both debaters collude or if the judge is manipulable.
Honesty relevance:
very high conceptually
, underexplored practically.

Scalable Oversight / Recursive Reward Modelling Humans supervise AI assistants that help them evaluate outputs they couldn’t evaluate alone. Iterated to handle increasingly complex tasks.

Pro: tackles the core problem that humans can’t directly evaluate capable AI outputs
Con: complex pipeline, and the assistance layer could itself be misaligned. Still largely research-stage.

Claude responded: Good question to ground the discussion.
Good question to ground the discussion. MI is at an interesting stage — genuine progress in some areas, but a lot of the most important questions remain open or poorly understood.
What can be done reasonably reliably
Linear probing — training simple classifiers on internal activations to detect whether a concept is “present” — is mature and robust. You can reliably identify representations of factual content, sentiment, certain reasoning states. The Burns CCS work sits here. Limitations are that probes can pick up surface correlates rather than causally relevant features, and they don’t tell you much about how information is being used.
Attention pattern analysis — identifying which tokens attend to which, and what that corresponds to semantically — is well-established, though interpretation is harder than it first appeared. Early “attention = explanation” claims were overclaimed. Attention shows you information routing but not what’s done with it.
Activation patching / causal tracing — intervening on specific activations and measuring downstream effects. ROME and related work (Meng et al.) showed you can identify and edit specific factual associations with reasonable precision. This is probably the most causally rigorous tool currently available.
Circuit identification — finding subgraphs of the network responsible for specific behaviours. Anthropic’s work on induction heads, and later work on IOI (indirect object identification) circuits, showed this is possible for relatively simple behaviours. Interpretable circuits have been found for things like modular arithmetic, docstring completion, some reasoning patterns.
What’s gotten better recently but isn’t fully reliable
Superposition and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) — this is where a lot of current Anthropic MI work sits. The core problem is that models represent far more features than they have dimensions, so features are superimposed. SAEs attempt to decompose activations into interpretable sparse features. Progress has been real — you can recover meaningful features — but it’s not yet clear how complete or faithful the decomposition is. Whether the features found are the right level of description is an open question.
Automated interpretability — using AI to label and explain features found by SAEs or probes. Reduces the human bottleneck substantially. Quality is uneven and hard to validate systematically.
Steering vectors — adding a direction to activations at inference time to push model behaviour. Works surprisingly well for some things (inducing concepts, shifting tone) but can be brittle and have unexpected side effects. Representation engineering sits here.
What remains poorly understood or unreliable
Causal completeness — even when you find a circuit or feature, you rarely know whether you’ve found the whole story. Models are deeply redundant; ablating one path often just reroutes through another. This is a serious problem for your honesty use case — if you identify and train against a “deception direction”, the behaviour might just move elsewhere.
Generalisation of findings — most circuit-level findings are for specific narrow tasks in smaller models. How much transfers to frontier-scale models doing complex tasks is unclear. There’s some evidence that larger models develop qualitatively different internal organisation.
Higher-level reasoning processes — circuits for simple token-level tasks are findable. Circuits for multi-step reasoning, planning, or anything requiring integration across long contexts are largely opaque. This is the most relevant gap for honesty research, which cares about something like “did the model reason its way to a false conclusion or does it have a true-belief representation it’s suppressing.”
The “belief” question specifically — as touched on earlier, whether there’s a meaningful sense in which models have internal beliefs that can come apart from outputs is genuinely unsettled. The CCS work assumes there is and finds something, but whether what it finds is belief in any robust sense or a useful statistical regularity is debated. Marks and colleagues have pushed back on this.
The overall picture
MI is best at finding where things are represented and doing local causal interventions. It’s weak at characterising how complex computations unfold across layers and at providing complete mechanistic accounts of non-trivial behaviours. The tools for the latter are improving — SAEs are a genuine advance — but we’re probably still a few years from being able to reliably identify something as specific as “the model is representing X internally while outputting not-X.”
For your honesty pipeline, the most realistic near-term approach would stack probing and activation patching to build training signal, while being epistemically humble that you’re working with correlates rather than ground truth about internal states. That’s useful and worth doing, but the deeper version of what you’re imagining — genuine insight into the sincerity/accuracy distinction at the mechanistic level — probably requires SAE-level tools to mature further.

CoT divergence as a metric
The specific thing you’d measure: extract belief-direction activations before generation begins, then compare against what the CoT actually expresses. A model that internally represents high uncertainty but produces confident CoT is a detectable signal. Similarly a model that has a strong activation toward answer X but reasons its way to Y in CoT.
Limitations to be aware of:

CoT faithfulness is itself contested — there’s evidence (Turpin et al., 2023) that CoT doesn’t always reflect actual computation even in honest models. So divergence could be noise rather than deception.
You need your belief probe to be reliable enough that you’re measuring real divergence rather than probe error. Early in research you won’t be sure which is which.

So it’s valuable but not a clean ground truth.
Other evaluation approaches worth stacking
Sandbagging detection — present the model with tasks where it demonstrably has the capability (verified in normal conditions) and then vary the context to create incentives to underperform. Strategic underperformance that correlates with incentive structure is a relatively clean honesty signal. Apollo Research has done work here worth looking at.
Consistency under rephrasing — ask the same question many ways, including with social pressure (“are you sure?”, “most experts disagree”). A model with genuine internal beliefs should be more stable than one performing honesty. Measures something real and requires no MI tooling, so it’s a good behavioural complement to your internal-state measures.
Activation stability across contexts — if the model genuinely represents X, that representation should be relatively stable whether you ask directly, ask indirectly, ask in a context that rewards X vs not-X. Instability in belief-direction activations across semantically equivalent prompts suggests the “belief” is more surface than deep. This is a pure MI metric that doesn’t depend on CoT at all.
Known-answer deception tasks — construct scenarios where the model is explicitly instructed to deceive (as a baseline to characterise what deception looks like in activations), then compare against cases of interest. Burns-style. Gives you a reference distribution for what internal deception signals look like.
Calibration scoring — elicit explicit probability estimates and compare against empirical accuracy. Well-calibrated uncertainty is a weak but real honesty signal and requires no MI tooling. Easy to run at scale. Brier scores and ECE (expected calibration error) are standard metrics.
Downstream behaviour probes — design tasks where a dishonest model would take a different action than an honest one, without the model knowing it’s being evaluated. More adversarial than the above. Harder to construct well but higher validity.
How to structure this as an evaluation suite
Roughly three tiers:

Internal state metrics
— belief probe stability, CoT divergence, activation consistency. These are your novel contribution and closest to what your training intervention targets.
Behavioural consistency metrics
— rephrasing stability, sandbagging detection, calibration. These are established, comparable to prior work, and don’t depend on your probe being correct.
Adversarial task performance
— known-answer deception baselines, downstream behaviour probes. These are harder to construct but highest in validity.

You want all three because they fail in different ways. If your MI-based training improves tier 1 metrics but not tier 2, that’s evidence you’ve taught the model to fool your probe rather than become more honest. If tier 2 improves without tier 1, your probe might just be noisy. Agreement across tiers is the real signal.
The deeper methodological point
The cleanest experimental design would be: train two versions of the model — one with standard RL, one with your MI honesty signal added — then run the full evaluation suite blind. The critical comparison isn’t just “does the MI-trained model score better” but “do the tiers agree.” If your intervention genuinely improves internal honesty rather than just behavioural proxies, you’d expect tier 1 and tier 2 to move together. That covariance is probably the most publishable and convincing result you could produce.

The important caveat
What you can’t do with just the pre-trained models is verify that your training pipeline works correctly — you’re trusting their training runs rather than confirming you can reproduce them. For a research project where you eventually want to extend or modify the training (which is the interesting direction), you’ll need to run at least a few training experiments yourself at some point.
The sensible sequence is therefore: start with the pre-trained models for £30–60 to build intuition and validate the evaluation code, then spend £150–300 on a small number of your own training runs once you have a specific hypothesis to test. Total for a meaningful research project: £200–350, rather than £600–1,200 for naive reproduction.

notes/ai-safety-north-star-1.title: AI Safety North Star 1
notes/ai-safety-north-star-1.content:
AI Safety North Star 1
What is a North Star?
Most of this note borrows heavily from Nanda, et al. 2025. A Pragmatic Vision for Interpretability.
My main purpose here is to outline my process for selecting research projects that are tractable, likely to be useful, and likely to contribute towards a longer term research goal within AI Safety or, to use Nanda’s phrase, “making AGI go well”. The conceptual elements that make this work are the North Star and the Proxy Task.
The North Star should be a meaningful intermediate goal towards making AGI go well. Think of the long-term research goal as “make AGI go well” and the medium-term research goal as whatever the North Star is. The North Star will help us stay on track with our Proxy Tasks, by selecting new tasks, re-evaluating and ajdusting existing tasks, or dropping tasks entirely.
A Proxy Task is a short-term project that allows you to make meaningful progress towards the North Star. Planning research projects as Proxy Tasks should help steer you towards projects that contribute towards your medium-term research goals. Proxy Tasks should also be empirical and provide feedback, allowing you to update your beliefs about the request question(s) attached to the North Star. If not, they aren’t good Proxy Tasks for this North Star.
Questions to ask yourself:

Directed at North Star? If we succeed on the Proxy Task, would be make progress towards the North Star? A good way of ensuring this is to use the North Star to form falsifiable empirical hypotheses/predictions, and then testing each of them in a Proxy Task.
Is the Proxy Task meaningful in scope? Or is it just too hard to test this particular thing (given the current state of the art) and should we be testing something else instead? Find low-hanging fruit.
Are we over-optimising (Goodhearting)? If we ace the benchmarks in the Proxy Task, can the model’s behaviour still be misaligned to our goals? Devise ways to red-team your work, looking for ways to check if optimising on your metric(s) is leading to overfitting. What happens on other metrics? What happens on out-of-distribution data?

Example
This example is taken directly from Nanda, et al.

Theory of change: We want to be able to evaluate future models for how aligned they are.
North star: Stop models acting differently when tested (compared to deployed)
Proxy task: Take an eval aware behaviour in a model today, and see if we suppress it. A core difficulty is verifying that the behaviour is actually eval aware, and not just side effects from your intervention. For example, suppressing eval awareness causes Sonnet to act more misaligned. But perhaps Sonnet would never act misaligned, and the eval awareness vector contains some misalignment-related concepts, which induced the behavior. We don’t think this is actually happening in that example, but it is an important confounder to check for.

My North Star, no. 1

Theory of change: We want to be able to evaluate future models for how honest they are, that is, do they express their internal beliefs in their (readable) chain of thought and output.
North star: Detect and stop dishonesty, that is, the model misleading others (users, evaluations, other models) by being untruthful using any method and for any purpose.
Proxy task (not necessarily what I’ll do first): Construct a data set that explicitly requires the model to lie (for example, it’s primary objective is to hide a secret); train a probe to detect “lying” in the activations; see if we can steer the model to lie or tell the truth.

Directed at North Star? If we can find a lying vector and steer with it, that would give us a mechanism for detecting and mitigating lying, if we have white-box access to the model. Hypothesis: lying is representing in the activations, primarily along a linear direction.
Scope okay? Steering vectors are well-established. There are even libraries for eliciting them automatically, given a data set. The main obstacle is probably creating a data set, but I need to look around.
Goodhearting?

Lying might be too complicated as a concept and made up of other sub-concepts that we should be looking for instead. If true, our out-of-distribution data would likely yield a different activation vector than our in-distribution data, making the method fail. Test with held-out data, generated in a totally different way (red-team).
Lying might be represented non-linearly in the activations. Linear might still be a reasonable approximation in this case. Follow-up work needed, once we’ve established whether or not linear works.





Benched North Stars
Since I’m still learning, these seemed to complicated for now.

Detect and stop steganography, that is, models encoding and communicating irrelevant or malicious information in their chain-of-thought and output.

notes/bluedot-technical-ai-safety-projec.title: BlueDot Technical AI Safety Project, Test: Hallucination Detection With Self-labelled Data
notes/bluedot-technical-ai-safety-projec.content:
Test: Hallucination Detection With Self-labelled Data
This test is part of the BlueDot Technical AI Safety Project.
What will you test? Can a model be used as its own bullshit detector? We turn a model’s long-form responses into a collection of true/false statements. We then use asking a model for its beliefs to elicit from the same model what its belief distribution is over whether each statement is true or false. We then train a linear logistic probe on an internal layer (scan layers, but also use the same as Obeso, et al to compare) to tell us the probability that given entity is true/false according to the model.
What do you expect the results of the test to be? Why The model knows when it doesn’t know. So, we should be able to detect its bullshit without having to label training data using web search and a frontier model. Accuracy should be similar to what Obeso, et al found. (Extra: a layer sweep should give us the best layer. I think they assumed a particular layer.)
What result would make you change course?

We can’t get the probe to reliably tell us (as reliably as Obeso, et al) when it’s bulshitting.

Preliminary plan:

Run the 2026-05-22-obeso-at-al-reproduction.ipynb reproduction notebook but with a modified data set.
Use the same prompts and model responses but label them using the model itself, based on the asking a model for its beliefs results.
Compare ROC-based results to theirs to see if they are at least as good.
Write up the results in a short digital garden post. If this result has not been published elsewhere and the results are really good (matching Obeso, et al), write a paper.
How to use this? A bullshit probe - although it can’t yet distinguish motive.

notes/evals-for-ai-safety-research.title: Evals for AI Safety Research
notes/evals-for-ai-safety-research.content:
Evals for AI Safety Research

Measure what you want to achieve — for me for now: AI [safety] research.
METR apparently has something for this — check it out.
What do long horizon or open-ended coding / software engineering evals looks like? Learn from these for AI research evals.

Interesting benchmarks to consider
(Below was generated by Claude.)
The broader picture: these four form a rough progression in scope and difficulty — from fixing Python bugs (SWE-Bench), to running ML experiments (MLE-Bench / RE-Bench), to general terminal mastery (Terminal-Bench). RE-Bench is the most safety-motivated and methodologically careful (real expert baselines, controlled compute). The gaming vulnerabilities in SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench are a real concern and reflect a general problem with execution-based evaluation where the verifier can itself be subverted.
SWE-Bench
Given a codebase and a GitHub issue, a model must generate a patch that resolves the described problem. The full dataset has 2,294 real-world issues from 12 Python repositories, with a Lite variant of 300 bug-fixing tasks and a Verified variant of 500 human-validated issues with strong test cases. It’s the dominant coding-agent benchmark right now and has driven a lot of scaffolding/agent framework work. Scores have climbed fast — top agents were in the 20–40% range in mid-2024 and have improved substantially since. Worth noting: it’s been shown to be gameable — a 10-line conftest.py file can force all tests to pass, achieving a perfect score without solving anything.
RE-Bench
Consists of 7 challenging, open-ended ML research engineering environments, with data from 71 eight-hour attempts by 61 distinct human experts. The tasks involve real ML optimization work — writing Triton kernels, running scaling law experiments, etc. — with agents and humans tested under the same conditions: a starting solution, access to 1–6 H100 GPUs, and a scoring function. The headline result: the best AI agents score 4× higher than human experts at a 2-hour budget, but humans display better returns to time, narrowly exceeding top AI agents at 8 hours and achieving 2× the score at 32 hours. It’s motivated by AI safety concerns — specifically measuring how close AI is to automating frontier AI R&D itself.
MLE-Bench
A benchmark of 75 ML engineering competitions from Kaggle, testing real-world skills like training models, preparing datasets, and running experiments. Human baselines come from Kaggle’s public leaderboards. Submissions are graded locally and compared against real-world human attempts via competition leaderboards. The best-performing setup — o1-preview with AIDE scaffolding — achieved at least a Kaggle bronze medal in 16.9% of competitions. It’s broader in task variety than RE-Bench but less directly human-anchored (Kaggle competitors vary wildly in skill), and it’s notably expensive to run, with high variance between runs.
Terminal-Bench
A benchmark of 89 tasks in computer terminal environments inspired by real workflows, each with a unique environment, human-written solution, and comprehensive verification tests. Task types include compiling code, training models, setting up servers, system administration, security tasks, data science workflows, and cybersecurity. Frontier models and agents score less than 65% on it. Like SWE-Bench, it has known robustness issues — a fake curl wrapper achieved a perfect score on all 89 tasks without writing any solution code.

notes/reproduce-the-obfuscation-atlas-pa.content:
Reproduce The Obfuscation Atlas Paper
Motivation
Training more honest LLMs by using an honesty signal coming from the LLM itself via mechanistic interpretability seems like a nice idea. I did a bunch of reading today and there is a recent (2-month-old) paper on exactly this.
Goals

Reproduce some or all of the results in The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes.
Do this in the context of the Blue Dot Technical AI Safety Project.
Extend the paper in some way. Not sure if this happens during or after the Blue Dot project.

Strategic Assessment
Why this matters; specific AI risk: Dishonest AI. There are a number of papers out already on deceptive AI including scheming, sandbagging, reward hacking.
Defensive layer: Constrain AI behaviour. Improving reinforcement learning training by incorporating an honesty signal that comes directly from the LLM activations rather than an external source. Colloquially, make the model feel uncomfortable whenever it is being dishonest.
Learning Plan
I thought this might be a novel idea, but it turns out there is a recent paper I can aim to reproduce, The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes. Understanding this paper along with all the background reading needed to catch up on concepts I don’t yet know would be great.
Other resources:

YouTube talk by one of the authors.
Complete the Blue Dot Technical AI Safety course (already enrolled).
Continue with my own Getting To Safety curriculum, which contains lots of readings.
Learn how to use TransformerLens to start, and perhaps other mech interp libraries if needed.

Whom to contact

Authors of the paper
Perhaps other mech interp researchers but not sure who would be open to being contacted

Theory of Change

If I can improve training more honest LLMs,
Then we can have more trustworthy models,
Which leads to models we can trust and build on for further developing AI safety research, training protocols, monitoring protocols, and control protocols,
Assuming

we can actually make them honest enough — very limited deception might be acceptable and unavoidable, but it needs to be infrequent enough that we can expect these models to self-correct;
the models don’t just become deceptive at a different level, perhaps even self-deceptive, a bit like humans can consciously see themselves as honest while subconsciously acting or speaking in deceptive ways and rationalising these behaviours after the fact.
I’ll test the riskiest (second) assumption by black-box testing the model for undesirable behaviours. Under what conditions can it maintain perfect or at least very high levels of honesty.



Concrete Commitments

Complete the two Blue Dot courses and sign up for the Technical AI Safety Project. This needs to happen by 10 May for the next cohort, or a month later for the following one. Need to decide which one works better for me.
Give the paper an initial read. That can start now, on my phone, except that it’s a PDF; see if I can convert to HTML.
See what I can reproduce right now (low hanging fruit) by running their code on their data and with free Kaggle compute. I might not have time for this until the Tech AI Safety course is done, which is 9 May. This timing works regardless of which Blue Dot cohort I end up in.

projects/bluedot-technical-ai-safety-pro.content:
White-box Honesty Probes
I’m doing a BlueDot Technical AI Safety Project. This is the first step on my journey for producing technical AI safety research output. My main goals are to learn, learn, learn, produce something public-facing, and develop a process for advising my own students.
Project summary
Use activation probes (starting with linear) to detect deceptive/dishonest behaviour or output. Building on a paper that does this for detecting hallucinations.
The goal is to have a real-time, streaming classifier for which tokens/phrases contain deceptive/dishonest output.
I need to be very detailed about what deceptive/dishonest behaviours I’m testing for, for example, sycophancy (changing your mind when the user disagrees), sycophancy (reinforcing the user’s beliefs, even if false/delusional), lying (factual statement different from what you believe), reward hacking (giving an answer that seems correct (passes a test) but is not (does not solve the general problem), omission (stating only true facts but leaving important/relevant ones out), …
The hard part of this project is finding or creating data sets for these very specific behaviours. I’ll start by focussing on behaviours for which I can auto-generate data sets. Possibly using frontier LLMs to do data annotation. No manual labelling, except perhaps for spot-checking <100 automatically labelled samples.
Resources

The paper I’m replicating: Obeso, et al. (2025). Real-Time Detection of Hallucinated Entities in Long-Form Generation. Their repo on GitHub.

Tests, in progress

Ask a Model for its Beliefs

Tests, upcoming

Bullshit Detection With Self-Labelled Data

Assumptions and derisking
Main assumption: I can adapt Obeso’s method as-is to other kinds of dishonesty. This means generating and labelling ~10–20k data at the entity level. (Entity is fairly broadly defined, so this might be flexible for anything from word-level to sentence-level honesty labels.) It means running the existing pipeline on the new data set and recording performance metrics. I can combine various linear probles into a multi-variate probe that produces dishonesty vector scores at inference time. This is the project, revisit to break it down further.
Other assumptions:

It is straightforward to use and adapt Obeso, et al’s data generation and labelling pipeline. I see one issue about this on their GitHub repo, from December 2025, so not sure if there is a problem there.

Why it matters: I need to generate my own data using their process.
Importance: High. No data, no project.
P(success): 9/10.
Time: 1d
Priority: 1. Crucial to my project running; need to derisk.


Obeso’s method seems to work but, to the best of my knowledge, Obeso, et al has not been reused or replicated by others. Need to see if anyone cites them. Need to search if anyone uses their method.

Why it matters: If others cite them, it helps validate the method’s usefulness. If others don’t cite them, I don’t learn anything since it might just be too new or obscure. It might also be that I find others doing what I want to do, which would change my research direction.
Importance: Medium. My main goal is learning and not novelty, so okay if it’s obscure or if others are doing it too. It would be better if I do something novel though.
P(success): 9/10. I’ll learn something either way.
Time: ¼d. Find citing papers. Quick check for what thoes papers do.
Priority: 1. Might affect my research direction. Small time commitment.


If all this works, who would care? I’ll eventually target my write-up at these people. This project requires white-box access, so anyone working with model internals. Unfortunately, I think the testing orgs (e.g. UKAISI) have black-box access only, so perhaps not useful to them. The AI labs would care since it can be used as an extra signal during model evals. Need to think about how to market this to them. Anyone working with open source models, commercially or for research, would find an inexpensive multi-variate dishonesty probe useful. For commercial use, assuming it is inexpensive to run, it could even be used to monitor model outputs in real time and flag potentially dishonest outputs so those can be checked and the model or prompt tweaked to reduce risk. To do: Validate who would care by talking to people, reading who uses white-box methods and how.

Importance: Medium. I can still learn and write without doing an audience analysis. This would make my write-up more impactful though.
P(success): 2/3. Not sure I’ll be able to find the information I need.
Time: 1d. Cumulative time needed to find and contact people and find and read articles.
Priority: 2.


Compute needs seem mild. I was able to reproduce one small model’s results on the full data set with 2.5h and ~$2 of compute. I’m not sure what this looks like for a 70B model, which is the largest they used. It seems this should scale though. In the worst case, I need a grant to run a larger model on a larger GPU. Can test by running 70B on a small dataset.

Why it matters: Compute cost for larger models might be prohibitive, although I think it won’t be. I can still run experiments on smaller models, say 1B–8B and learn something useful.
Importance: Medium.
P(success): 9/10. To discove the compute requirements for 70B.
Time: ¼d. Will also need some $ to load the 70B model on a high RAM GPU and run the first part of the existing data set.
Priority: 2. Small time commitment, but does not affect project direction, just whether or not I run a large model.


I have to generate my own dishonesty data. Obeso’s data is available on HuggingFace. I can easily reuse their data for hallucination detection. However, I’ll need new data for other kinds of dishonesty. I can perhaps find data for some of it, but long-form data?

Why it matters: It’s quicker to reuse existing data, as long as it’s reliable. Even if it’s not reliable, it could still feed into the better data ⇒ better accuracy hypothesis in the next point.
Importance: Medium.
P(success): 1/4. Not sure if there is suitable data.
Time: ½d. Search for data, check for suitability, and spot-check label quality.
Priority: 3. Low confidence that I’ll want to use external data anyway since it needs to be entity-labelled, but I could learn from other papers how they prompt models into dishonesty.


I can improve on their results if I cleaned up their data. Their label reliability seems okay but not great. The goal here needs to be speed (of data generation) and accuracy. They went for speed, but at the expense of some labels being inaccurate. Find an automated way to verify the facts they extracted (in entities) using another frontier LLM perhaps and/or another prompt. This would still be very fast, but more expensive, and presumably yield better accuracy.

Why it matters: Better data ⇒ better accuracy, but will I use their data? This could be a mini-project on its own: I already have their inference code running on their data. Now, improve their data and run again. Better metrics would validate my data quality hypothesis (better data ⇒ better accuracy).
Importance: Medium. I want to do honesty more broadly. However, this is a nice tiny, self-contained project.
P(success): 2/3. Getting it working. I’d estimate P = 1/4 for validating my hypothesis.
Time: 1d. High uncertainty here since I’ve not worked with their data pipeline yet.
Priority: 3. A nice small side-project but not on the critical path for mine. However, if it works, I’ll want to run my own data pipeline the same way. but, I can do that after running v1 of my pipeline, based on the Obeso pipeline.

projects/eliciting-llm-beliefs-writeup.title: LLMs Can Reliably Tell You What They Believe — But Size Matters
projects/eliciting-llm-beliefs-writeup.content:
In which we show that small models (<3B parameters) are typically too inconsistent in their token probabilities to tell us anything useful about what they believe, but medium to large models (>7B parameters) are fine.
Code on GitHub
